newsitem.title: CHINA: China bank reserve cut seen not to loosen credit.
newsitem.headline: China bank reserve cut seen not to loosen credit.

text.p: China's planned cut in bank reserve requirement ratios would not lead to an easing of a tight monetary policy, the official Economic Daily said on Thursday.
"Will the cut in bank reserve ratios be a sign of easing in credit? The answer is no," the newspaper said.

The central bank, the People's Bank of China, currently requires commercial banks to keep 13 percent of deposits as reserves with a further five to seven percent as separate provision funds. These funds are held by the central bank, which pays 8.28 percent interest on them.
China's central bank governor Dai Xianglong has announced a plan to cut the 13 percent reserve ratio, but has stressed that the cut would not herald an easing of tight monetary policy.
The central bank may cut the reserve ratio to about 10 percent, officials have said.
The central bank would recall loans extended to commercial banks after the reserve ratio cut and issue financing bills to banks to offset the amount of reserves released, the newspaper said.
China has kept a tight rein on monetary policy since mid-1993 to cool inflation, but cut interest rates twice last year to ease interest burden on state firms.
The central bank has said it will maintain an "appropriately tight" monetary policy.
